title: Memento — saved values, private state, and restoration
author: Dr. Charles Dorner

slides.title: Undo must restore a valid pair, not two guesses
keyPoints: The interval is inclusive and stays within 0 through 100
The low endpoint never exceeds the high endpoint
A history manager should not expose private state
slides.narration: A chart selection is an interval with two endpoints. Restoring only its low endpoint could combine an old low with a new high and create a state that never existed. The real requirement is to remember a valid pair and restore that pair together under the object's rules. For a local procedure, two copied integers may be sufficient. The design pressure arrives when the selection has private state and several callers need history. Making those fields public just to help undo weakens the rest of the program. We need the state owner to create a saved record while allowing the history manager to store that record without understanding its contents.
actions: Ask learners to state the invariant before suggesting storage.

question.prompt: What exactly is the state boundary of the chapter snapshot?
question.answer: The selected interval’s low and high endpoints. It does not include chart pixels, mouse position, external files, or history length.

slides.title: Copying two local values is a sound baseline
keyPoints: Remember the pair before the change
A copied value does not follow later edits
Restore both values from the same saved moment
slides.narration: The baseline works with ordinary local integers because there is no private object boundary to protect yet. old_low and old_high copy the original interval. The selection then moves to twenty and forty, and the two saved values still hold two and five. Restoring both returns the original pair. This establishes the core behavior before introducing any pattern: saved state must be independent of future edits. The code does not provide range checking or a history container, so do not mistake this tiny demonstration for the full Selection design. Its purpose is to show why copying values works. The later snapshot type adds control over who can create and inspect those saved records.
actions: Predict the changed and restored pairs before Run.

question.prompt: Why does changing low to twenty leave old_low at two?
question.answer: old_low holds an independent copied integer, not a reference to low.

slides.title: A reference is not a photograph of the past
keyPoints: A reference is another name for the live value
The alias changes when the current value changes
A snapshot must own the state it promises to remember
slides.narration: This program keeps both an alias and a copy. int& names an existing integer, so aliased_low remains tied to low. When low becomes twenty, reading the alias also gives twenty. copied_low still gives two. Every access here is safe because the original integer stays alive; the failure is logical, not a dangling-reference trick. A snapshot built from references to the live endpoints would have the same defect. It would appear to save successfully while forgetting the past as soon as the selection changed. Memento needs independent state or carefully shared immutable state. Borrowing mutable current state is not enough just because the wrapper is named Snapshot.
actions: Run and explain why both outputs are valid C++ but only one satisfies history.

question.prompt: Which saved value could restore the original low endpoint after this change?
question.answer: copied_low. aliased_low reads the new current value and no longer represents the old state.

slides.title: Let the object define its saved record
keyPoints: Selection creates and restores valid snapshots
Snapshot hides the endpoint representation
History stores records without opening them
slides.narration: Memento is a saved record controlled by the object whose state it represents. Selection is often called the originator: it knows how to produce and restore the record. History is the caretaker: it keeps snapshots and chooses which one to use. Those names describe responsibilities, not required base classes. In the chapter, History never reaches into the two endpoint fields. That separation matters when Selection later gains another part of its state. The change can stay inside Selection and Snapshot rather than spreading through every undo manager. A snapshot still needs a declared boundary. Hiding fields does not answer whether a new property should be restored; the product's undo promise must answer that question.
actions: Ask what changes if a selection later includes a display mode.

question.prompt: Why should History avoid reading the endpoint fields even if it could copy them?
question.answer: Selection owns the representation and invariants. Opaque records keep history independent of changes to that representation.

slides.title: The contract we must preserve
keyPoints: Maintain 0 <= low <= high <= 100.
Capture and restore both endpoints as one logical state.
Let History store records without reading their private values.
slides.narration:
An opaque snapshot of a valid chart interval. Selection creates a private nested Snapshot containing copied integers. History owns snapshots by value and borrows the selection. Restoration leaves the snapshot reusable and history consumes a record only after restore.

Maintain 0 <= low <= high <= 100. Capture and restore both endpoints as one logical state. Let History store records without reading their private values.

Every Selection pair is valid before and after public operations. A saved snapshot is unaffected by later changes to its source. History must not outlive the Selection it borrows. Cross-instance restore is allowed because instances share the same value rules. These are the rules that define a correct extension, even if it has the right C++ types. For one local edit, saving two old integers is enough. Command-specific inverse operations can reduce storage for large changes, but require correct reverse behavior. Shared immutable snapshots help large documents at the cost of more ownership design.

question.prompt: Which promise would a new Memento implementation be allowed to break?
question.answer: None of the stated requirements. The implementation may change, but these rules remain: Every Selection pair is valid before and after public operations. A saved snapshot is unaffected by later changes to its source. History must not outlive the Selection it borrows. Cross-instance restore is allowed because instances share the same value rules.

slides.title: The problem: remember an interval without breaking its rules
keyPoints: A chart lets a reader select an inclusive interval from zero through one hundred.
Exposing low_ and high_ so a history manager can copy them creates two risks.
slides.narration:
A chart lets a reader select an inclusive interval from zero through one hundred. The low endpoint must never exceed the high endpoint. A change sets both endpoints together, and undo should restore the previous pair. One direct approach keeps two old integer variables beside the user-interface code. That is enough for a single local operation when the state is already public. The problem appears when the selection owns private state and more callers need undo without learning how that state is stored.

Exposing low_ and high_ so a history manager can copy them creates two risks. A caller can change only one endpoint and leave an invalid interval. Also, adding another part of selection state forces every outside snapshot routine to change. The object that understands the rules should produce its own saved record. The history manager should store that record without reading or editing its contents. A saved record with this role is a memento, also called a snapshot.

question.prompt: An interval changes from 2:5 to 20:40. What information is needed to restore the earlier selection?
question.answer: The earlier pair, two and five, must have been saved. Keeping only the new pair or a reference to the changing pair does not preserve the previous state.

slides.title: Let the state owner define the snapshot boundary
keyPoints: Selection keeps low_ and high_ private.
Snapshot publicly supports copying.
slides.narration:
Selection keeps low_ and high_ private. Its set operation accepts both values, validates all conditions, and changes neither member if the pair is invalid. The Snapshot nested class also keeps its two integers private. Its constructor is private, so outside code cannot construct an arbitrary invalid pair disguised as a valid snapshot. friend class Selection grants Selection access to those private members and constructor. Friendship is a specific access permission; it is not inheritance, ownership, or a promise that all surrounding classes can inspect the record.

Snapshot publicly supports copying. This lets a History store snapshots in a vector without seeing their fields. Selection::save builds a snapshot from the current valid pair and returns it by value. Modern C++ can construct that returned value directly in its destination; whether a small copy is removed does not change the ownership contract. The snapshot owns two independent integers, so later edits to Selection cannot change what the snapshot remembers. A snapshot that stored references to live endpoints would fail this basic requirement.

slides.title: Restoration should have a clear failure story
keyPoints: restore takes a const Snapshot& and copies both integers back.
The snapshot stores the entire selected interval and nothing else.
slides.narration:
restore takes a const Snapshot& and copies both integers back. It borrows the saved record for the duration of the call and leaves that record unchanged. Because these integer assignments cannot allocate or throw, restoration cannot stop between endpoints through a C++ exception in this implementation. This is an exception-safety guarantee for local operations, not a statement that another thread cannot see an intermediate assignment. The program is single-threaded and requires external synchronization if shared.

The snapshot stores the entire selected interval and nothing else. It does not store the chart pixels, a mouse position, a disk file, or the number of saved history entries. Those choices form the snapshot boundary: which state is restored together. Including too little produces inconsistent restoration; including unrelated state makes undo surprisingly broad. Here any Snapshot created by any Selection can be restored into another Selection because every instance uses the same range rules. The test demonstrates that portable value policy. A per-document or per-session policy would need an identity token and an explicit rejection rule.

slides.title: The history manager keeps records without opening them
keyPoints: History borrows a Selection and owns a vector of Snapshot values.
In this example restoration cannot throw, but retaining the order makes later changes easier to reason about.
slides.narration:
History borrows a Selection and owns a vector of Snapshot values. remember asks the selection for a snapshot and stores it. undo returns false for an empty vector, making the lack of history an ordinary result rather than an exceptional failure. Otherwise it restores the last snapshot and only then removes that snapshot. The order expresses a useful general rule: do not consume the recovery record before the restoration it supports has succeeded.

In this example restoration cannot throw, but retaining the order makes later changes easier to reason about. If snapshots later include a string or collection, restoring field by field could allocate and fail halfway through. A stronger design could build a complete proposed state first and swap it into place with a nonthrowing operation. The caretaker, the common pattern name for a history manager, should not guess how to do that. The object that owns the state must preserve its own invariants during restoration.

slides.title: A snapshot is a value, not a rewind button for the world
keyPoints: The sample saves [2,5], changes the selection to [20,40], and restores [2,5].
Restoring an interval does not undo an exported image that was already sent to another person.
slides.narration:
The sample saves [2,5], changes the selection to [20,40], and restores [2,5]. It also keeps a separate snapshot variable and restores it more than once. This is valid because restore does not consume the snapshot. History choosing to pop its last record is a policy of that history, not a property of all snapshots. A history can instead support named checkpoints, multiple branches, or repeated restore to one baseline. Each needs a clear rule for which records remain available.

Restoring an interval does not undo an exported image that was already sent to another person. A snapshot covers local state inside its declared boundary. It also does not automatically provide persistence across program runs: the program stores C++ values in memory and defines no file format. Persistent snapshots need versioned data, validated loading, and a plan for fields that change between software versions. Calling a memory snapshot a backup would mislead users unless those additional guarantees exist.

slides.title: Bound memory growth without weakening the contract
keyPoints: Unlimited history stores more records after every remember call.
A complete copied snapshot is easiest to reason about but may be costly.
slides.narration:
Unlimited history stores more records after every remember call. For two integers this seems cheap, but a rich document may hold large images or trees. A capacity limit is therefore a product choice as well as a memory choice: the user can undo only so far. The lab retains the newest three remembered states. It builds a proposed vector, removes the oldest item if necessary, appends the new snapshot, then swaps the proposed vector into place. If allocation fails before the swap, the original history remains available.

A complete copied snapshot is easiest to reason about but may be costly. An alternative stores only the changed values, called a delta, or uses command-specific undo as in Chapter 14. Another approach shares immutable data between snapshots. These designs can save memory but add dependencies between records or more demanding ownership rules. Measure the actual state size and editing pattern. Do not replace a few cheap copied values with a complicated history graph merely because the latter sounds more advanced.

question.prompt: Why validate a pair before assigning either endpoint?
question.answer: The relation low <= high spans both values. Partial assignment followed by rejection could leave an invalid interval even though the operation reported failure.

slides.title: Private construction protects the saved-state boundary
keyPoints: Snapshot fields and constructor are private
friend class Selection grants specific access
Public copying lets History store opaque values
slides.narration: Snapshot is nested within Selection, but the key access permission is explicit: friend class Selection allows Selection to use Snapshot's private constructor and fields. Friendship is not inheritance, ownership, or permission for every nearby class. Outside callers cannot manufacture an arbitrary invalid endpoint pair as a Snapshot. They can copy an existing snapshot because its copy operations are public. That distinction lets a vector manage records while keeping their contents opaque. The compiler enforces these access restrictions when building the program. The valid-pair guarantee also relies on Selection::set validating all conditions before changing either live endpoint; access control alone does not make arbitrary implementation code correct.
actions: Separate permission to copy a record from permission to construct arbitrary contents.

question.prompt: Can History create a Snapshot containing low nine and high three through the private constructor?
question.answer: No. Only the granted friend can call that constructor. History can store copies of snapshots Selection has produced.

slides.title: Validation happens before either endpoint changes
keyPoints: Reject low below zero
Reject high above one hundred or low above high
A rejected set leaves the previous pair intact
slides.narration: The interval invariant is a relationship between the two integers, not a rule on either integer alone. Selection::set checks the proposed pair before assigning low_ or high_. If it rejected only after writing low_, an invalid request such as nine and three could damage the current state even though the caller receives an exception. The actual source throws first and leaves the earlier pair untouched. This behavior makes snapshots trustworthy: save reads a state that successful operations preserve as valid. While stepping through the code, identify where validation ends and mutation begins. That boundary is often more useful in a review than counting how many guard statements a function contains.
actions: Trace the invalid request and identify the first assignment that must not execute.

question.prompt: After rejecting set(9,3) while the selection is [2,5], what should save remember?
question.answer: [2,5]. Rejection must leave both prior endpoints unchanged.

slides.title: Restore a value; do not consume the record
keyPoints: const Snapshot& borrows an unchanged record
Integer copies restore the pair without allocation
This implementation permits cross-selection restoration
slides.narration: restore takes a const reference, so it borrows the record during the call and does not edit it through that reference. The two integer assignments do not allocate or throw, which gives this small restoration a clear exception-safety story. It does not make the assignments atomic to another thread; the example is single-threaded. The same snapshot can be restored repeatedly, and another Selection can restore it because all instances share the same range rules. If records belonged to one document or session, the design would need an identity token and a checked rejection policy. Do not silently impose that different policy on this source: portable saved values are an intentional tested behavior here.
actions: Distinguish repeated restore of one value from consuming an undo-history entry.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch17.json → Restoration should have a clear failure story

question.prompt: Does restoring a snapshot remove or invalidate that snapshot?
question.answer: No. restore borrows it unchanged. History’s choice to pop a record is a separate policy.

slides.title: Keep the recovery record until restoration succeeds
keyPoints: Empty history returns false
Restore the newest record first
Remove it only after successful restoration
slides.narration: History owns a vector of snapshots and borrows the Selection it manages. undo first handles the normal empty case by returning false. Otherwise it restores the last record and then pops it. That order means the recovery record remains available until the operation it supports has succeeded. In this integer example, restoration cannot throw, but the order communicates a useful rule for future state. If restoration later copied strings one field at a time, allocation could fail midway. Selection would need a stronger strategy, such as building a complete proposed state and committing it safely. History should not guess how to repair partially restored private fields; that responsibility stays with the state owner.
actions: Ask what a future throwing restore would lose if the record were popped first.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch17.json → The history manager keeps records without opening them

question.prompt: Why should pop_back follow restore rather than precede it?
question.answer: A failed restoration should not first destroy the record needed for recovery. The current nonthrowing integer restore also preserves this clear ordering for maintenance.

slides.title: Bounded history needs a commit point too
keyPoints: Retain the newest three records
Build changes in a proposed vector
Swap only after the new history is ready
slides.narration: A capacity limit is visible behavior: it determines how far a user can undo. The extension keeps the three newest remembered states. It copies the current records to proposed, removes the oldest there if necessary, adds the new record, and swaps proposed into the live history. Allocation failure before that swap leaves the old history intact. This is a small example of preparing a new state before committing it. It costs a copy, which is reasonable for a teaching history of two-integer records. A fixed-capacity buffer may be faster for large or frequent updates, but its overwrite order needs equal care. Performance changes should preserve the same eviction and failure contract.
actions: Have learners trace the proposed vector before the final swap.

question.prompt: After remembering [1,2], [2,3], [3,4], [4,5], which record has been evicted?
question.answer: [1,2]. Undo visits [4,5], [3,4], then [2,3], and then reports no history.

slides.title: Map the roles to the actual types
keyPoints: Originator → Selection
Memento → Selection::Snapshot
Caretaker → History
Client → main
slides.narration:
Originator → Selection. Own current state and define save/restore operations. Selection validates both endpoints together and decides the snapshot boundary.

Memento → Selection::Snapshot. Retain an independent state record. The new nested value has private endpoints and a private constructor.

Caretaker → History. Keep records in order and decide when to restore one. History cannot inspect or edit snapshot endpoints.

Client → main. Choose when to remember relative to edits. A snapshot taken before a change records a different checkpoint from one taken afterward.

The originator controls access and restoration rules.
A history manager can store opaque records.

slides.narration:
A snapshot should own the state it promises to remember. The originator controls access and restoration rules. A history manager can store opaque records. State boundaries determine what undo actually restores. Local memory snapshots do not imply persistent backups or reversal of external effects.

The state owner retains control of representation and valid restoration. Whenever a new field is added, review whether it belongs inside the snapshot boundary and add a restore test for that choice.

question.prompt: Explain Memento without reciting its class names.
question.answer: Selection creates a private nested Snapshot containing copied integers. History owns snapshots by value and borrows the selection. Restoration leaves the snapshot reusable and history consumes a record only after restore. For one local edit, saving two old integers is enough. Command-specific inverse operations can reduce storage for large changes, but require correct reverse behavior. Shared immutable snapshots help large documents at the cost of more ownership design.

slides.title: A snapshot, a delta, or an undo command?
keyPoints: Full values make independence easy to reason about
Deltas can save space but depend on context
Commands remember actions and their reversal data
slides.narration: For two integers, copying complete state is clear and cheap. A large document may need a different tradeoff. A delta stores only a change, but rebuilding a state can depend on earlier records remaining available. Shared immutable data can avoid repeated copies, provided later edits never mutate the data old snapshots share. A Command remembers an action and enough information to reverse its successful effect. These designs can also be combined: a command may ask an object for a snapshot before changing it. Choose based on measured state size, edit frequency, and the undo promise. Replacing a tiny value record with a complicated history graph can increase both bugs and explanation cost without a practical benefit.
actions: Compare restoring one standalone pair with replaying several changes.

question.prompt: What is the main new dependency introduced by storing only deltas?
question.answer: Restoration may require a valid earlier state or chain of earlier records. Each delta is not necessarily an independent complete snapshot.

slides.title: Do not call a memory snapshot a complete backup
keyPoints: Only state inside the boundary is restored
External effects are not reversed automatically
Persistent records need a format and version policy
slides.narration: Restoring the selected interval does not unsend an exported chart. The saved record covers local endpoints only. It also disappears when the process ends because this program defines no persistent file format. A durable backup would need serialization, validated loading, and a policy for changes between software versions. These limits are not failures of Memento; they are limits of the promise actually implemented. When undo looks wrong, ask first whether the missing state was inside the snapshot boundary, whether it was copied or merely aliased, and whether the history still retained the desired record. Those questions distinguish a faulty implementation from an unsupported expectation.
actions: Ask learners to name one external effect that endpoint restoration cannot reverse.

question.prompt: Will a Selection snapshot restore the number of entries already removed from History?
question.answer: No. History length is outside this snapshot’s state boundary.

slides.title: Explain remembered state without exposing it
keyPoints: The originator knows the representation
The caretaker owns opaque history records
Restoration preserves the originator’s invariant
slides.narration: Retell the design from the user's action. Before an edit, the state owner creates a valid saved record. A history manager stores that value without learning its fields. After the edit, the manager can ask the owner to restore the record. The owner alone knows how to make that transition while preserving its rules. That explanation captures Memento more accurately than saying undo copies some data. Transfer the lesson to a game checkpoint: decide whether score, position, random-generator state, and inventory belong in one boundary. Omitting a related part can produce a state that never existed. Including unrelated external actions can promise a reversal the program cannot deliver.
actions: Give a checkpoint example and ask learners to defend its state boundary.

question.prompt: What must be decided before writing a snapshot type for a larger object?
question.answer: Which state must be restored together, who may create valid records, how restoration can fail, and how record lifetime and retention work.

graph.title: History holds records; Selection defines their meaning
graph.caption: The History-to-Snapshot edge means owned value storage. History-to-Selection is a borrowed dependency. Selection can read Snapshot internals because of friendship, a C++ access rule; the creation/read arrow is a teaching dependency and does not mean Selection owns every saved snapshot.
